511.quote_or_event: “After listening to scriptures, a person comes to know what is good and what is sinful, having thus known through listening one ought to perform what leads to welfare.”
511.explanation: This Dasavaikalika verse, gathered in the Saman Suttam, teaches that one should come to know both the good and the harmful and then choose to do what leads to welfare.
511.tie_back: The kural asks for the person who weighs both good and harm and is drawn to the good; the Jain verse describes exactly that act of knowing both sides and then choosing the beneficial.
511.source: Saman Suttam v. 245 (Precepts on Right Knowledge; from Dasavaikalika Sutra 4.11; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
511._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com; the Dasavaikalika origin is the standard identification of the Prakrit gatha, not separately checked. Near one-to-one on weighing both sides and choosing the good, though framed as spiritual rather than administrative.

512.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men.”
512.explanation: Before his renunciation, Rishabha, the first Tirthankara and first king, is credited with giving people the arts, crafts and occupations by which they live.
512.tie_back: The kural praises the administrator who widens the sources of income and builds prosperity; Jain tradition gives its first king the role of founding the arts and occupations on which prosperity rests.
512.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
512._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Thematically related (creating livelihoods for the people), but it concerns a founding king's teaching, not a revenue officer's skills, and Jainism ultimately values his renunciation over the reign.

513.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
513.explanation: Of the four passions (kashayas) that bind karma, greed is singled out as the one that ruins every virtue.
513.tie_back: Freedom from greed is one of the four qualities the kural requires before trust; the Jain verse explains why it matters so much, since greed undoes everything else, love included.
513.source: Saman Suttam v. 135 (Precepts on Passions; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
513._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. Matches one of the four qualities (freedom from greed) strongly and touches love; knowledge and firm judgment are not covered.

514.quote_or_event: “After they have been instructed, admitted into the order, and nourished with food and drink, they disperse in all directions like geese whose wings have grown.”
514.explanation: The teacher Garga laments pupils who were instructed, accepted and cared for, yet once in service would not carry out their tasks and scattered.
514.tie_back: The kural observes that many people tested and approved still turn out differently once they are doing the work; Garga's pupils, received and trained with care, prove exactly that.
514.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
514._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close fit on people accepted after preparation who change in practice; the kural's emphasis on prior testing is implied rather than explicit.

515.quote_or_event: “An excellent pupil needs no express directions, or he is (at least) quickly directed; he always carries out his duties as he is told.”
515.explanation: The lecture on discipline describes the worthy disciple as one who understands what is required and reliably carries it through.
515.tie_back: The kural would give a task only to one who knows how to do it and can see it through, not to a favourite; the Jain verse describes that kind of capable, reliable doer.
515.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
515._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Matches the positive standard of competence and follow-through; the warning against favouritism is absent.

516.quote_or_event: “At the right time a monk should sally forth, and he should return at the right time; avoiding to do anything out of time, he should do what is appropriate for each period of the day.”
516.explanation: Jain monastic discipline insists that each action be fitted to its proper time.
516.tie_back: The kural's third step is to act when doer and deed fit the right time; the Jain rule makes timeliness a matter of discipline, though it does not address sizing up doer and deed.
516.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
516._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Matches only the timing element of the kural's three-part method.

517.quote_or_event: “'What shall I do now? I want to be employed, sir, in doing some work or in studying.' If he is ordered to do some work, he should do it without tiring; if he is ordered to study, he should do it without allowing himself to be affected by any pains.”
517.explanation: In the daily routine of the Jain monk, the superior assigns each disciple either work or study, and the disciple carries out the assigned task fully.
517.tie_back: The kural says that once you have decided who will do a task, you should hand it over to him; the Jain routine shows a superior assigning work and the disciple taking it on wholly.
517.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 26.9-10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
517._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Shows the assigning of work, but the kural's point, leaving the task with the chosen man after deliberate matching, is only partly reflected.

518.quote_or_event: “At last he anointed his hundred sons as kings, and gave each a kingdom.”
518.explanation: Before renouncing the world, Rishabha handed over rule by consecrating his sons and giving each a realm of his own.
518.tie_back: The kural asks that a man found fit for a task be made its rightful holder with full authority; Rishabha's act of anointing each son over his own kingdom is a formal transfer of authority of exactly that kind.
518.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
518._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Shows a transfer of authority, but the Kalpa Sutra says nothing of first testing the sons' fitness, and the context is renunciation.

519.quote_or_event: “(A bad pupil thinks:) 'I get but knocks and boxes on the ear, hard words and blows;' and he believes a teacher who instructs him well, to be a malevolent man.”
519.explanation: The lecture on discipline describes the bad pupil who misreads the well-meant care of a devoted teacher as hostility.
519.tie_back: The kural warns the ruler who misreads a devoted worker's closeness and grows suspicious of him; the Jain verse shows the same error of turning genuine devotion into imagined ill will, though here it runs from pupil to teacher.
519.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
519._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The error is the same (misreading devotion as malice), but the roles are reversed and the kural's consequence, loss of fortune, is absent.

520.quote_or_event: “Then he should, in due order, reflect on all transgressions he has committed during the day, with regard to knowledge, faith, and conduct.”
520.explanation: Jain monastic practice prescribes a daily review (pratikramana) in which each monk examines and confesses the day's lapses before his guru.
520.tie_back: The kural asks the king to examine his workers' conduct every day so that nothing goes crooked; Jain discipline builds the same daily inspection into every monk's evening routine.
520.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 26.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
520._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong on daily scrutiny of conduct, but it is self-examination with confession to the guru (26.41) rather than a ruler supervising officials.
